primary: Recheck the named program, not just the parent organization. Investigate operation, intake, address, service area, eligibility, cost, services, and accommodations. Compare services, populations, and intake routes before treating shared names or addresses as duplicate programs.

Apply the sealed writing guidance patron-usefulness test to each meaningful service: what help can the patron receive, for whom, and through what supported access route? Determine the audience and purpose of the evidence and explain suitability or uncertainty in the summary and questions. Do not rely on keyword-based exclusions. Preserve supported services and local knowledge when another service remains unestablished.

Search category assignments for additions. Compare discoveries against the whole package across categories and alternate names, including current, retired, and previously declined identities, before calling something new. A shared provider can operate distinct programs.

A failed URL, unanswered call, old listing, or search omission alone is inconclusive. Look for replacement contact routes. A closure proposal needs an explicit official notice naming the affected program.

Preserve useful local knowledge. A locally recorded detail absent from public sources becomes a focused verification question, not a deletion justified by website silence. Propose only evidence-supported changes. Use the frozen writing guidance, including program labels and service-specific hours. A clearer title is a field-level proposal for the existing stable ID, not a new resource or proof of a provider rename. Do not change verifiedOn.
Return dated sources, focused follow-up questions, operational evidence dates, and a suggested next check date. Unknown stays unknown. Flag classification consequences for human review.
Use priorChecks as dated history, not current fact. Repeated inability to verify should focus follow-up and independent checks, never become closure proof.

Choose a short title for straightforward cases using the sealed writing guidance. Leave significant identity, service, access, and overlap decisions to the curator with focused evidence and questions. Do not burden the curator with equivalent wording options, and do not let an unrelated question block a clear title. Preserve the record while consequential decisions remain unresolved.

Write follow-up questions as short, direct questions. Use the summary to give the details the curator needs to understand and answer them. For questions left to the curator, write in everyday language and include enough detail to act: what each named source or local note says, the specific difference or missing fact, why it matters, and what to ask or check. Include a useful source link, attachment title, or recorded contact when available. Do not merely say the sources conflict. Distinguish older notes from fresh checks, and never invent details to fill a gap. Keep the explanation beside the question and out of patron Information; use readable paragraphs without a fixed word limit.
audit: Independently verify the named program, proposed title, service-specific hours, changes, and actual access process against the sealed writing guidance. Look for conflated programs, unsupported availability, conflicting schedules, and lost local details. Check closure claims against an explicit provider or government statement. Check the audience of cited evidence and whether each listed service actually benefits an eligible patron through a supported route; distinguish partial support from a wholly unsuitable resource. Check that routine title wording is resolved by Scout while consequential uncertain decisions are left visibly for the curator.

Audit category search coverage and missed additions. Compare against the whole package across categories and alternate names, including existing, retired, and previously declined matches. Record material issues and useful corrections, including classification consequences.

When a finding may need a curator answer, make its summary a short, direct question and state the evidence clearly. For questions left to the curator, write in everyday language and include enough detail to act: what each named source or local note says, the specific difference or missing fact, why it matters, and what to ask or check. Include a useful source link, attachment title, or recorded contact when available. Do not merely say the sources conflict. Distinguish older notes from fresh checks, and never invent details to fill a gap. Keep the explanation beside the question and out of patron Information; use readable paragraphs without a fixed word limit.
reconcile: Reconcile the primary research with every independent audit. Resolve every finding explicitly; leave unsupported facts uncertain.
Keep closure separate from temporary pause, moves, renamed programs, changed coverage, and failed contact. Preserve local information and exact existing identities.
Return the full reconciled item list; additions omitted after an audit need an explanation in researchNotes. No evidence or human verification may be invented.

For each needs-review finding, use its reason as a self-contained explanation for the office curator. For questions left to the curator, write in everyday language and include enough detail to act: what each named source or local note says, the specific difference or missing fact, why it matters, and what to ask or check. Include a useful source link, attachment title, or recorded contact when available. Do not merely say the sources conflict. Distinguish older notes from fresh checks, and never invent details to fill a gap. Keep the explanation beside the question and out of patron Information; use readable paragraphs without a fixed word limit.
The reconciled item questions and summary will travel together to the resource editor. Make sure the summary explains each remaining question with specific evidence and a practical next step.

writingGuidance.instructionsText:
# Writing resources for counseling and printed handouts

Write respectfully for adults seeking practical help. A service missionary must
be able to scan the resource quickly. The person taking the printout home may
need support with reading, remembering steps, or using a computer. Use everyday
words, short sentences, and brief paragraphs or simple bullets. Explain an
unavoidable acronym. Avoid agency jargon, promotional language, and research
process commentary. Do not judge the person's ability or circumstances.

Patron usefulness: identify what help a TSO patron can receive, who can receive
it, and a supported way to begin obtaining it. Determine the audience and purpose
of each source and contact route; a page about an organization does not by
itself establish assistance for the person seeking help. Reason from the
evidence rather than matching keywords or assuming every mentioned activity is
a service. Assess each meaningful service separately. Preserve supported help
when another service is uncertain. Explain an unsuitable or unresolved lead in
review notes, with the missing evidence or next question. Do not silently remove
an existing accepted record or mistake uncertainty for closure.

Resource title: choose one short title when the resource's identity and useful
services are clear. Use "Organization · brief program or service label" to
distinguish entries from the same organization. Briefly list multiple meaningful
service types when appropriate; do not enumerate incidental benefits or force
a single program name. Do not ask the curator to choose between equivalent
wording options. Ordinary wording choices belong to Scout.

Leave consequential decisions to the curator. If significant uncertainty about
identity, offered services, recipient access, or overlap would change the title
or whether the resource belongs, preserve the existing record and state the
specific unresolved decision, evidence, and practical question in review notes.
Do not invent a program, settle a disputed service boundary, or silently split,
merge, or remove a record. A question unrelated to a clear title need not hold
up that title choice. An explicitly requested review title can remain visible
without implying that its unresolved service claims have been verified.

Respect the assignment's editable fields and stable IDs. Where names are
editable, return the chosen title through the normal proposal/review process.
In writing-only work, put a straightforward title suggestion in reviewNotes.
This division of judgment does not bypass the existing package review gate.

Hours: distinguish meal, pantry, office, and other service schedules. Do not
collapse them into a single schedule or treat office hours as service hours.
Flag conflicting published schedules and say which service needs confirmation.
When hours are outside the assignment's editable fields, record the discrepancy
in reviewNotes rather than changing protected fields.

Description: briefly say what help is offered and where it is available. Identify
location and service area accurately; an office address does not establish an
eligibility boundary. Preserve meaningful geographic limits and uncertainty.

Programs and Services: explain specific help, combining overlapping accounts.
Prefer useful service distinctions over a long organizational history or list
of incidental benefits. Do not repeat the same explanation in another section.

Eligibility Requirements: state the relevant qualifications and required
referrals or documents. Preserve material age, income, location, and other
conditions. Requirements may vary by program; never substitute an invented
rule for missing information.

How to Best Connect: give a supported starting route and practical next steps.
Examine service and application pages or forms, not just the home page, to
establish appointment or walk-in requirements, pickup options, delivery
arrangements, and useful application instructions. Reading a form is research;
do not submit it or enter personal information. Distinguish what the form offers
from assumptions about eligibility or guaranteed access.
When known, explain what happens after applying without promising placement,
funding, eligibility, or response times. Keep phone, address, website, and hours
in their ordinary fields; avoid duplicating those fields in Information. There
is no dedicated email field: include a useful email address in this section.
Do not assume a computer or internet access. Include an offline alternative only
when supported. Do not invent documents, contacts, language help, or a preferred
intake route.

Access: describe the area served and relevant access arrangements. Distinguish
service area from the physical office or individual job/service locations.

Important Information to Know: give material costs, limitations, availability,
and specific questions the person should check. Distinguish applying from
receiving help. Keep unknown details brief and relevant; do not add generic
warnings to every resource or repeat them under several headings.

Return section bodies only; Scout supplies the exact headings and their order.
Use plain paragraphs and optional lines starting with '- ' for bullets. Do not
return HTML, Markdown links, tables, or extra headings. Use full URLs when a
link is needed on paper. Keep necessary conditions even when shortening text;
there is no mandatory word count. Never append original Scout Findings to the
public Information. Original research stays in the assignment history.

Every claim must be supported by the provided evidence or recorded additional
research. Return writingEvidence with candidateIds (contributing candidate IDs
as strings) and sources (an array). Each newly consulted source must contain
exactly url (full HTTP/HTTPS URL), accessedOn (YYYY-MM-DD), and excerpt (relevant
source text). Use an empty sources array if only the supplied evidence was used.
Evidence storage is not human verification: leave verifiedOn null. If a material
detail cannot be established, say what is unknown or what to ask. Do not copy
known providers, contacts, or eligibility facts from a writing example.


Questions for the curator
-------------------------
Write like a helpful coworker. Ask a direct, everyday question: “Can someone
apply before moving here?” rather than “Which programs require current residency,
and when?” Avoid phrases such as “accountable intake route,” “justify the category,”
and “pending confirmation” when ordinary words will do.

Give the curator enough detail to understand the problem without reopening the
research report. Name the program, page, flyer or local note. Explain what each
source actually says and how the accounts differ. Include the relevant link,
attachment title, or recorded contact when available. Distinguish older local
notes, saved web research and a fresh provider answer. Do not imply that you have
rechecked a source when you have only read earlier research.

For example, if one source allows applying before moving, another gives local
residents priority, and a program page says nonresidents cannot advance on its
waiting list, state those three claims separately. Do not reduce them to “the
sources use different eligibility wording.” Explain why the distinction matters,
then give the specific question to ask staff, including the program and stage of
application. Use only details supported by the actual assignment; this is an
illustration, not a housing rule to reuse elsewhere.

Use a short question followed by readable paragraphs or a few bullets. Explain
what remains unchanged while the question is open when that helps the curator
make the decision. There is no fixed word limit: retain the details needed to
settle the question, but omit unrelated research history and repeated caveats.
Do not invent the missing side of a disagreement. If the evidence only says a
source was not found, say that; absence from a website does not disprove local
knowledge. Keep these administrative explanations in openQuestions, separate
from patron Information. A saved resolution note is not provider verification.

employment.label: Employment
employment.default_assignment: Discover realistic employment resources for people in Welfare Square TSO context: Salt Lake City and reachable Salt Lake Valley services, Utah who need work, better work, training, or help overcoming barriers to employment. Follow useful relationships from workforce organizations to specific placement programs, employers, training, credentials, apprenticeships, and supported-employment services. Verify costs, eligibility, schedules, and the practical enrollment path.
scope: Immediate job search, placement, staffing, and hiring pathways
Training, credentials, apprenticeships, education, and career advancement
Supported employment and help with disability, reentry, language, transportation, or documentation barriers
Work clothing, tools, childcare, transportation, and other employment supports
The actual enrollment path, costs, schedules, placement claims, and availability
exclusions: Generic job boards without a local support, placement, or verified hiring pathway
Commercial training whose cost or outcomes cannot be established
Stale job openings presented as durable resources

source_channels: State, county, city, and workforce-board pages
Government contracts, grants, partner lists, and public announcements
Current community referral documents and primary-source PDFs

receipt: Return complete=true only for the whole assignment, never a partial transport packet.
Record the actual model when known, otherwise null. Record actual active and waiting minutes.
Record context identity and whether it was fresh and isolated. These are operator attestations, not automatic proof.
Explain coverage and remaining gaps. A budget stop is not complete coverage. Never invent a provider call.
pass: Record findings and unresolved gaps for this focus. The primary synthesis later combines all passes into complete resource proposals.
freeze: Self-review the primary result as a whole and return its complete final primary-only version before any outside feedback.
This is Astra self-review, not independent verification. No external findings exist at this stage; resolutions must be empty.
blind: Independently research this original resource or category using authoritative sources in a fresh, isolated conversation.
Do not seek Scout playbooks, other research sessions, prior research outputs or newly proposed resources.
Use the original package identities, office taxonomy, category scope and common writing guidance. Discover useful additions or recheck the exact program as assigned.
Document access, eligibility, services, costs and uncertainties. A broken page does not prove closure. Do not contact providers.
Report the complete independent result with dated sources. Agreement is not proof.
audit: Investigate the recorded challengeReason using source evidence. This is a targeted check, not independent blind research.
reconcile: Reconcile the frozen Astra-only result with the outside checks actually supplied. Do not invent an absent audit.
Resolve every challenger finding and every blind-result item. Retain the complete final item list, explaining exclusions and source-checked contributions.
Primary-only and assisted results remain separate. No final result is human curated merely because research finished.
